body_markdown:
Nobody quits on a Tuesday in November. At least not out loud.


But the resignation letter that lands on your desk the first week of January? It was written in November. Maybe not on paper. It was written in your leasing agent's head, in your maintenance tech's group chat, in the quiet moment your community manager decided these holidays would be her last ones with your company.


Turnover has a season. If you manage properties, that season is about to start.


##


**Why November is Decision Month for Resignations**


Think about what's happening on site right now. Renewals are piling up for year-end. Leasing traffic slows, so the pressure shifts to hitting occupancy goals with fewer prospects. Maintenance teams are winterizing, chasing heat calls, and covering for techs who already used up their PTO. Everyone is tired.


Then the holidays show up, and people finally get time to think. They see family. They compare notes with friends. They start asking one simple question: do I want to do this again next year?


Add a few practical triggers to the mix:


-


**Bonus timing:** Plenty of on-site pros wait to collect a year-end bonus before giving notice. The decision is made long before the check clears.


-


**New-year budgets:** Competitors open fresh headcount in January, and recruiters start calling your best people in December.


-


**Fresh-start energy:** January is when people chase new goals. A new job is an easy one to put on the list.


So by the time someone walks into your office with two weeks' notice, the reason is usually two months old.


##


**The Real Cost of a January Exit**


Losing a team member hurts in any month. Losing one in January stings a little more. You head into spring leasing season short-handed, and the math isn't kind.


Maintenance technicians turn over at about 39% a year, the highest of any multifamily role, while the industry as a whole runs near 33%, according to


[National Apartment Association data](https://multifamilydive.com/news/maintenance-worker-employee-retention/694130) **.** Each exit carries a price tag, too. Research from the


[Center for American Progress](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/there-are-significant-business-costs-to-replacing-employees/) puts the typical cost of replacing a worker earning under $50,000 at roughly 20% of their annual salary, before you count the overtime it takes to cover the gap.


Residents feel it fast. Teams that respond to requests within two hours keep resident satisfaction near 92%, compared with about 83% for teams that take up to a full day, according to


[Kingsley survey data](https://www.multifamilyexecutive.com/property-management/kingsley-renter-satisfaction-holds-steady-renewal-intent-drops-slightly_o) . Short-staffed teams rarely hit that two-hour mark. Then, your remaining staff absorbs the extra work, burnout creeps in, and suddenly one resignation turns into three.


And the ripple doesn't stop with your team. Companies with staff turnover under 20% kept about 60% of their residents, versus 54% for companies above 20%, according to


****[Zego's State of Resident Experience report](https://www.multifamilyexecutive.com/property-management/75-of-multifamily-operators-say-renter-expectations-have-increased_o) **.** With each resident move-out costing


****[close to $3,900](https://www.multifamilydive.com/news/turnover-costs-4000-apartment-multifamily/696298/) **,** a handful of lost renewals can quickly outweigh what it would have cost to keep your people.


Open on-site roles show up everywhere, including in resident reviews, renewal rates, and the overtime line of your budget. But the fix isn't just faster hiring. It's spotting the risk while you can still do something about it.


##


**Five Moves to Make This Month**


**1. Hold stay conversations, not exit interviews:** Sit down one-on-one with your on-site team before the holidays. Ask what's working, what's frustrating, and what would make next year better. Then actually follow up. People stay where they feel heard.


**2. Spread the year-end load:** If your leasing team is buried in renewals and your maintenance crew is drowning in work orders,


[bring in temporary support now](https://propmgtdiv.bgsf.com/) . A few extra hands in November and December can be the difference between a tired team and an absent team.


**3. Get specific with recognition:** A generic "thanks for all you do" email won't cut it. Call out the tech who handled the 2 a.m. leak. Thank the leasing agent who saved a tough renewal. Specific praise sticks, while vague praise evaporates.


**4. Show people where they're headed:** Many on-site pros leave because they can't see a next step. Map out what growth looks like, whether that's assistant manager, lead tech, or a certification you'll help pay for.


**5. Build your bench before you need it:** Even with your best efforts, some people will leave. Line up qualified leasing agents, maintenance techs, and managers now, so a January resignation is a hiccup instead of a crisis.


##


**Plan for January in November**


Here's the good news: a decision made in November can still be changed in November. The window is open right now, but it won't stay open long.


Your on-site team is the reason your communities run. They take the 2 a.m. calls, save the tough renewals, and turn a building into a place people want to live. A stay conversation this week costs you an hour. Losing them in January costs you months of scrambling, a dip in resident satisfaction, and far more than a recruiting fee.


So don't wait for the letters to land. Talk to your people, lighten the year-end load, and line up your bench. Make January the month your team comes back recharged, not the month it walks out the door.
